Documenting Data with the DGF

documenting-data.Rmd

Documentation as filling in the blanks

Machines can measure and type a column, but they cannot know that grade is coded 1 = Freshman … 4 = Senior, or that rev means net revenue in thousands of dollars. That meaning has to come from a person. datagoodr’s approach is to make supplying it as light as possible: create_dgf() pre-builds the template fields for documentation, and you fill them in — in a spreadsheet.

The division of labor is clean: the machine measures and types; the human supplies the meaning the data cannot carry on its own.

The dictionary fields

Every variable’s row carries data-dictionary cells waiting for text:

  • dd_vlabel — a short human label,
  • dd_vdesc — a longer description,
  • dd_vname_alias — an alternate name, if the source uses one.

You edit them where the DGF lives — in Excel, or programmatically — and they belong to the variable from then on.

The factor template: the real time-saver

The field that saves the most work is the one for factors. When a column is categorical, create_dgf() does not just note “categorical” — it enumerates the levels into dd_f_levels as a template, one entry per level, each waiting for a human-readable label and definition. A coded column arrives in the DGF already expanded into the rows you need to annotate:

# dd_f_levels for `grade`, as created — a template to fill in:
  level   label        definition
  1       ___          ___
  2       ___          ___
  3       ___          ___
  4       ___          ___

# after you edit it in the spreadsheet:
  level   label        definition
  1       Freshman     first-year undergraduate
  2       Sophomore    second-year undergraduate
  3       Junior       third-year undergraduate
  4       Senior       fourth-year undergraduate

You never have to discover the levels yourself or build the table — you only supply the words.

How the entries become documentation

The text you add in these fields is not inert; it flows into both outputs:

  • The rendered Research Guide. The labels and descriptions become the headings and prose of the profile, and the factor level labels replace the raw codes in the category table and treemap — so 1/2/3/4 reads as Freshman/Sophomore/Junior/Senior in the published guide.
  • The governed CSV. The portable families of the DGF — the dd_ dictionary, the stable_ descriptors, and the validate_ rules — are embedded in the governed CSV written by write_stable_csv(). So the labels and definitions travel with the data to the next tool or repository, not as a detachable sidecar, and map cleanly toward archival standards (such as DDI) for deposit.

Why edit in a spreadsheet

Keeping documentation in the DGF — a table you open in Excel — is deliberate. It is where analysts already work, it needs no new tool or query language, and a colleague who does not use R can still read, review, and contribute. That is the whole premise: governance and documentation that meet people where they are.

Re-profiling with update_dgf() preserves every hand-edited label and definition, so documentation accumulates as the data evolves rather than being redone each cycle.

Where this fits

This closes the loop the guide has walked through: Getting Started and The datagoodr Workflow for the shape of it; Rule-Based Data Governance for the why; Stabilizing Datasets, Data Profiling, and Profiles & Research Guides for the machine-produced half; and this vignette for the human half that turns a profiled dataset into finished, shareable documentation.
